content:
Your church needs records that support its tax-exempt status and any federal returns it must file. IRS guidance includes governing documents, minutes, accounting records and property records, even when a church has not applied for formal recognition of exemption.

Start a corporate records binder with those documents, and keep a clear index to related files. Use the filing arrangement below as a practical starting point, then check the rules that apply to your church.

---

## Choose a usable filing system

The IRS does not prescribe a specific recordkeeping format for churches. Choose a system suited to your activities, with records that support the income and expenses in your books.

For this setup, use a binder for permanent corporate documents and an index to financial and property files stored elsewhere. Give each index entry a document category and its storage location. Keep the same categories in your electronic folders so you can find the supporting records when needed.

<Callout type="tip">
This binder layout is an organizing suggestion. The IRS requires adequate records, not a particular binder, set of tabs or software product.
</Callout>

---

## Gather the permanent documents

IRS Publication 4221-PC recommends keeping organizing documents, amendments and board minutes permanently. It also includes the application for recognition of exemption and the determination letter among permanent records.

Create these tabs or folders:

- Articles of incorporation or other organizing document, with amendments.
- Bylaws, with amendments.
- Board meeting minutes.
- Exemption application and IRS determination letter, if your church has them.

Keep earlier amendments with the permanent documents. Mark the current governing documents clearly so a reader can distinguish them from older versions.

The IRS church guide says recordkeeping applies whether or not the IRS has officially recognized your exemption. If your church has no determination letter, continue collecting the records that support its claim to exemption.

---

## File decisions as they happen

The IRS encourages governing bodies and authorized committees to document meetings and written actions contemporaneously. File the resulting minutes and written decisions with the governance records.

Check your own state's nonprofit corporation law for the records it requires. For example, Washington's corporate-records statute covers meeting minutes, unanimous written consents and actions by board committees. It also calls for current governing documents, a current director and officer list, and the latest annual report delivered to the secretary of state.

Use that example to prepare questions for your state filing office or attorney. Confirm which records your legal structure must maintain, rather than treating another state's checklist as your own.

---

## Keep the supporting records

Your accounting books need supporting documents. IRS examples include invoices, paid bills, receipts, deposit slips and canceled checks. Organize those files by year and type of receipt or expense, and put their locations in the binder index.

Retain documents showing the amounts and sources of receipts, including donor correspondence and pledge documents when applicable. For expenses, keep evidence of the amount paid and the purpose of the expense, including relevant contracts and invoices.

For property, keep acquisition and disposition records. Include purchase and sale documents, improvement costs and financing documents where applicable. File them by asset so the purchase history remains connected to the eventual disposition record.

---

## Set retention periods carefully

Use the IRS guidance below as a starting point for your written retention schedule. These are different categories with different starting events, not a single discard date for everything in the binder.

| Record category | IRS guidance |
|---|---|
| Organizing documents, bylaws and amendments; board minutes; exemption application and determination letter | Keep permanently, under Publication 4221-PC guidance. |
| Revenue and expense records, including payroll records | Publication 1828 says at least four years after filing the returns to which they relate. |
| Records of property acquisition and disposition, including investments | Publication 1828 says at least four years after filing the return for the year in which disposition occurs. |
| Employment tax records | The IRS employment-tax page says at least four years after filing the fourth quarter for the year. Special tax-credit records can require longer. |

The revenue and expense guidance is tied to the relevant return's filing. The property guidance is tied to the return for the disposition year. If no relevant return is required, ask your tax adviser how to set the retention period; do not invent a filing date.

<Callout type="important">
Retention guidance checked October 15, 2026. Before disposing of records, confirm the current guidance with the IRS and check applicable state requirements. Publication 4221-PC notes that a grantor, insurer, creditor or state agency may require longer retention.
</Callout>

---

## Protect paper and electronic files

Keep sensitive paper records in a locked cabinet or room. Limit access to people who need the information for their responsibilities, following the FTC's practical data-security guidance.

Apply that approach to payroll and other files containing personal information. Use the binder index to point to restricted files rather than putting every sensitive document into a widely shared binder.

Electronic records still need to meet the basic recordkeeping requirements that apply to paper records. The IRS encourages a written retention policy that addresses electronic files, backups, archiving and regular checks of system reliability.

<Callout type="warning">
A scanned file still needs protection and a usable backup process. Include backup and reliability checks in your records policy, and check access to sensitive files rather than assuming everyone with the binder needs those files too.
</Callout>

---

## Write down how records are handled

Adopt a written policy covering document integrity, retention and destruction, as the IRS encourages. Identify the categories you keep, their locations, the applicable retention periods and how you will dispose of sensitive records securely when they are no longer needed.

Include the electronic-file procedures and backup checks. Review access when people's responsibilities change so access continues to match their work.

Before approving destruction, check both tax and non-tax needs. Reaching the end of an IRS period does not settle a longer requirement from another applicable source.

---

## Check the binder against the files

Use this setup checklist:

- [ ] Gather organizing documents, bylaws, amendments and board minutes.
- [ ] Add exemption application records and the determination letter if applicable.
- [ ] Check state requirements for corporate records and current officer information.
- [ ] Index the accounting support and property records by storage location.
- [ ] Record retention periods and the events that start them.
- [ ] Restrict sensitive files and document backup and disposal procedures.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
excerpt: Organize your church’s governing documents, minutes and supporting records, with IRS retention guidance and a practical setup checklist.
title: Keeping a Corporate Records Binder

sources.claim: Opening: churches must retain records supporting exemption and required returns, regardless of formal recognition; required record categories. Sections 1 and 2: no prescribed format, applicable records even without a determination letter.
sources.quote: All tax-exempt organizations, including churches and religious organizations (regardless of whether tax-exempt status has been officially recognized by the IRS), are required to maintain books of accounting and other records necessary to justify their claim for exemption in the event of an audit.

sources.claim: Opening and sections 1, 4 and 8: the proposed binder/index layout organizes necessary records; it is an editorial application of the IRS requirement, not a mandated layout.
sources.quote: There is no specific format for keeping records. However, the types of required records frequently include organizing documents (charter, constitution, articles of incorporation) and bylaws, minute books, property records, general ledgers, receipts and disbursements journals, payroll records, banking records and invoices.

sources.claim: Section 1: choose a system suited to church activities that supports income and expenses.
sources.quote: A public charity can choose any recordkeeping system, suited to its activities, that clearly shows the organization’s income and expenses.

sources.claim: Section 2 permanent-document list, preservation of amendments, section 5 permanent-record row and section 8 first two checklist items. Marking current copies is a filing suggestion that preserves the permanent record.
sources.quote: Some records should be kept permanently. These include the application for recognition of tax-exempt status, the determination letter recognizing tax-exempt status and organizing documents, such as articles of incorporation and bylaws, with amendments, as well as board minutes.

sources.claim: Section 3: promptly document meetings and written decisions, including authorized committees.
sources.quote: The Internal Revenue Service encourages the governing bodies and authorized sub-committees to take steps to ensure that minutes of their meetings, and actions taken by written action or outside of meetings, are contemporaneously documented.

sources.claim: Section 3: Washington-only examples of required decision records. No Washington retention period is prescribed in this article.
sources.quote: Minutes of all meetings of its members and of its board of directors;

sources.claim: Section 3: Washington-only written consents and committee actions.
sources.quote: A record of all actions taken by the members and board of directors by unanimous written consent;

sources.claim: Section 3: Washington-only committee actions.
sources.quote: A record of all actions taken on behalf of the corporation by a committee of the board.

sources.claim: Sections 2, 3 and 8: Washington example calls for current governing documents and current officer/director details; distinguish current documents as an editorial filing suggestion.
sources.quote: Its articles of incorporation or restated articles of incorporation and all amendments to them currently in effect;

sources.claim: Section 3 Washington example of current bylaws.
sources.quote: Its bylaws or restated bylaws and all amendments to them currently in effect;

sources.claim: Sections 3 and 8: current director/officer list, Washington only.
sources.quote: A list of the names and business addresses of its current directors and officers;

sources.claim: Section 3: latest annual report, Washington only.
sources.quote: Its most recent annual report delivered to the secretary of state under RCW

sources.claim: Sections 3 and 8: consult applicable state requirements; do not generalize the Washington example.
sources.quote: State law often prescribes the type of organizational document and its content.

sources.claim: Section 4: accounting support list and suggested year/type filing structure; indexing locations is an editorial application.
sources.quote: Supporting documents include sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, and canceled checks.

sources.claim: Section 4: organize support documents by year and receipt/expense type.
sources.quote: For instance, organize them by year and type of income or expense.

sources.claim: Section 4: donor correspondence and pledge documents substantiate sources and amounts of receipts.
sources.quote: Documents that show gross receipts include: donor correspondence, pledge documents, cash register tapes, bank deposit slips, receipt books, invoices, credit card charge slips and Forms 1099-MISC, Miscellaneous Income.

sources.claim: Section 4: expense documentation needs amount and purpose; contracts and invoices support expenses.
sources.quote: Supporting documents should show the amount paid and the purpose of the expense.

sources.claim: Section 4: contracts among expense-support documents.
sources.quote: contracts, account statements, credit card sales slips, invoices

sources.claim: Section 4 property files: acquisition/disposition, improvements and financing. Filing by asset is an editorial way to preserve that history.
sources.quote: Documents that may show the above information include: purchase and sales invoices, real estate closing statements, canceled checks and financing documents.

sources.claim: Section 4: keep improvement costs and asset acquisition/disposition details.
sources.quote: Cost of any improvements

sources.claim: Section 5: revenue and expense guidance, including payroll, exact four-year period tied to filing related returns. Where no return is required the article refers to a tax adviser instead of inventing a start date.
sources.quote: Records of revenue and expenses, including payroll records. Retain for at least four years after filing the returns to which they relate.

sources.claim: Section 5: property acquisition/disposition, including investments, exact four-year period tied to filing the disposition-year return.
sources.quote: Records relating to acquisition and disposition of property (real and personal, including investments). Retain for at least four years after the filing of the return for the year in which disposition occurs.

sources.claim: Section 5: employment-tax four-year minimum tied exactly to fourth-quarter filing.
sources.quote: Keep all records of employment taxes for at least four years after filing the 4th quarter for the year.

sources.claim: Section 5: special tax-credit records may require longer; no credit-specific deadline is prescribed.
sources.quote: Records related to qualified sick leave wages and qualified family leave wages for leave taken after March 31, 2021, and records related to qualified wages for the employee retention credit paid after June 30, 2021, should be kept for at least 6 years.

sources.claim: Sections 5 and 7: check non-tax and state obligations before disposal; IRS periods do not override longer applicable needs.
sources.quote: For example, a grantor, insurance company, creditor or state agency may require that records be kept longer than the IRS requires.

sources.claim: Section 6: practical security recommendation to lock sensitive paper records and limit access; not a claim that FTC business-specific jurisdiction universally applies to churches.
sources.quote: Store paper documents or files, as well as thumb drives and backups containing personally identifiable information in a locked room or in a locked file cabinet.

sources.claim: Sections 6, 7 and 8: restrict payroll and personal-information records by work responsibilities; use index references instead of sharing sensitive contents; review permissions when responsibilities change.
sources.quote: That means each employee should have access only to those resources needed to do their particular job.

sources.claim: Section 6: electronic records meet the same basic requirements as paper.
sources.quote: All requirements that apply to hard copy books and records also apply to electronic records.

sources.claim: Sections 6, 7 and 8: written policy, electronic files, backups, archives, integrity and reliability checks.
sources.quote: The Internal Revenue Service encourages charities to adopt a written policy establishing standards for document integrity, retention, and destruction. The document retention policy should include guidelines for handling electronic files. The policy should cover backup procedures, archiving of documents, and regular check-ups of the reliability of the system.

sources.claim: Sections 7 and 8: record categories, retention, security and secure disposal in a written policy.
sources.quote: If you must keep information for business reasons or to comply with the law, develop a written records retention policy to identify what information must be kept, how to secure it, how long to keep it, and how to dispose of it securely when you no longer need it.

sources.claim: Required scripture callout, checked one verse on the publisher single-verse page; quotation only, no new theological interpretation.

sources.quote: But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner.

claim_check.notes: Writer opened all eight source URLs and checked retention wording and the single LSB verse. Independent Opus sentence-by-sentence source, scripture and screenshot review is pending; this is not author approval.

rulings: Map backlog how-to to allowed how_to; use phase 0 from the Legal section. The binder/index layout is a filing suggestion derived from recordkeeping guidance, not a legal mandate.

Use church-specific Publication 1828 retention guidance instead of the general three-year discussion. Preserve each starting event; do not infer a disposal date when no relevant return is filed. Cite Washington solely as a state-law example, without state retention periods.

Include no formation instructions, payroll setup, tax-credit eligibility, legal-hold advice or nationwide state-law claims. Security recommendations adapt FTC business guidance without asserting universal church jurisdiction. No theology, pastoral-care or methodology ruling is needed.
